overview: The Idrisids were a dynasty of the western Maghreb, established when Idris I gained support at Walila, the former Roman city of Volubilis, in 788 to 789. Their state depended on local Amazigh communities and alliances. The map’s label “caliphate” and interval 800 to 1000 simplify a changing network of rulers, towns and territories.

periods.title: Formation and expansion
periods.summary: Idris I and Idris II established rule and expanded their political network; Walila and Fez were important centres.

periods.title: Divided rule and outside pressure
periods.summary: The dynasty divided into branches and later faced competing Fatimid and Cordoban Umayyad power.

sections.title: A town larger than its Roman past

items.text: Walila did not begin with Idris I. Archaeologists distinguish earlier settlement from the enlarged town of the late eighth and ninth centuries. This matters because a Roman column reused in a medieval wall does not make the household living behind it Roman.

In the Idrisid-period quarter outside Walila’s walls, new houses had several rooms, and older buildings were enlarged or divided. Some courtyards contained wells. One house had an entrance that turned before reaching the interior, interrupting a direct view in from the street.

A furnace, ash pits and worked animal bones reveal craft activity in that quarter. Researchers interpret some of the bones as anvils used while making the serrated edges of sickles. The interpretation connects excavated workshop debris to agricultural tools, rather than to a royal treasure.

Simple houses excavated inside the walls had beaten-earth floors and small grain silos suitable for household storage. The much larger stores in a separate elite complex suggest different scales of food management. Archaeology lets us compare homes without pretending that every family lived alike.

A courtyard complex outside the walls had a kitchen, storage areas and an elaborate reception room. Its identification as a residence of Idris I or Idris II is a scholarly proposal, not a name written on the doorway.

Fez grew from two early settlements on opposite sides of a river, associated with Andalusian and Kairouanese quarters. The early city developed between 789 and 808; the two parts were enclosed together under later Almoravid rulers. Today’s medina therefore contains several historical layers.

sections.title: Bath time, game time and writing

items.text: Walila’s bathhouse, built in the late eighth or ninth century, included a cold pool and heated rooms. It places bathing within the material record of the early Islamic town. The building eventually ceased to function as a bath, so later finds require careful dating.

Someone cut a small board into a step beside the bath’s cold pool: three rows of at least thirteen holes, about 34 by 10 centimetres overall. Waiting for a bath could apparently include a game. The holes survive; the players and their exact rules do not.

Researchers compare the board with tab or sig games but do not claim a certain identification. Two bone dice from other buildings at Walila give additional evidence of play. They were not excavated with the bathhouse board, so we should not invent a complete boxed game.

A silver coin of Idris II in the Jordan Ahli Bank catalogue carries علي, “Ali,” in Arabic. This is a short name, shown here in ordinary modern type from the catalogue transcription. Its presence invoked the dynasty’s descent from Ali; it is not evidence that every inhabitant could read.

Coins were political messages as well as money. Idrisid silver named rulers and religious claims, giving contemporary evidence that can be compared with stories written centuries later. Their inscriptions also help identify mints and political connections.

Burnt and collapsed deposits in Walila’s outer quarter contain locally made pots and coins of Muhammad ibn Idris, who ruled from 828 to 836. These finds date a change in occupation. The fire alone cannot identify an attacker or explain the ending of the entire dynasty.

ending.text: During the tenth century, Idrisid rulers repeatedly faced Fatimid and Cordoban Umayyad intervention, with changing allegiances and periods of exile. Al-Hasan’s final attempt to return ended in defeat and death in 985. The dynasty’s political defeat did not remove the people, towns or religious memory associated with it.
